claim: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more human deaths each year than influenza.
source: Although respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is responsible for more human deaths each year than influenza, its pathogenic mechanisms are poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but is presented as established fact.

claim: RSV infection induces microtubule/dynein-dependent mitochondrial perinuclear clustering.
source: Here high-resolution quantitative imaging, bioenergetics measurements and mitochondrial membrane potential- and redox-sensitive dyes are used to define RSV's impact on host mitochondria for the first time, delineating RSV-induced microtubule/dynein-dependent mitochondrial perinuclear clustering, and translocation towards the microtubule-organizing centre.
evidence: The manuscript presents imaging data (Figures 1-4) and quantitative analysis showing mitochondrial clustering, and demonstrates this is dependent on microtubules and dynein through drug inhibition and siRNA experiments.

claim: RSV infection causes translocation of mitochondria towards the microtubule-organizing centre.
source: Here high-resolution quantitative imaging, bioenergetics measurements and mitochondrial membrane potential- and redox-sensitive dyes are used to define RSV's impact on host mitochondria for the first time, delineating RSV-induced microtubule/dynein-dependent mitochondrial perinuclear clustering, and translocation towards the microtubule-organizing centre.
evidence: Figure 2 shows mitochondrial distribution relative to the MTOC with quantitative analysis demonstrating increased mitochondrial signal within 45° of the MTOC at 18 and 24 h p.i.

claim: RSV infection impairs mitochondrial respiration.
source: These changes are concomitant with impaired mitochondrial respiration, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and increased production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: Figure 5 shows Seahorse bioenergetics analysis demonstrating decreased OCR (oxygen consumption rate) in RSV-infected cells over time.

claim: RSV infection causes loss of mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: These changes are concomitant with impaired mitochondrial respiration, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and increased production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: Figure 6 shows TMRE staining demonstrating reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in RSV-infected cells at 18 and 24 h p.i.

claim: RSV infection increases production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: These changes are concomitant with impaired mitochondrial respiration, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and increased production of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: Figure 7 shows FRR2 ratiometric imaging and FACS analysis demonstrating increased mitochondrial ROS in RSV-infected cells.

claim: Agents that target microtubule integrity strongly suppress RSV virus production.
source: Strikingly, agents that target microtubule integrity the dynein motor protein, or inhibit mitochondrial ROS production strongly suppresses RSV virus production, including in a mouse model with concomitantly reduced virus-induced lung inflammation.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows that nocodazole treatment significantly reduces infectious virus production by up to 2.5 log.

claim: Agents that target the dynein motor protein strongly suppress RSV virus production.
source: Strikingly, agents that target microtubule integrity the dynein motor protein, or inhibit mitochondrial ROS production strongly suppresses RSV virus production, including in a mouse model with concomitantly reduced virus-induced lung inflammation.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows EHNA treatment significantly reduces infectious virus production, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows siRNA knockdown of dynein components reduces virus production by 2-3 logs.

claim: Agents that inhibit mitochondrial ROS production strongly suppress RSV virus production.
source: Strikingly, agents that target microtubule integrity the dynein motor protein, or inhibit mitochondrial ROS production strongly suppresses RSV virus production, including in a mouse model with concomitantly reduced virus-induced lung inflammation.
evidence: Figure 7E shows MitoQ treatment reduces viral RNA copy number by up to 60% and infectious virus production by up to 3.5 logs at 24 h p.i.

claim: MitoQ reduces virus-induced lung inflammation in a mouse model.
source: Strikingly, agents that target microtubule integrity the dynein motor protein, or inhibit mitochondrial ROS production strongly suppresses RSV virus production, including in a mouse model with concomitantly reduced virus-induced lung inflammation.
evidence: Figure 9 shows that MitoQ treatment in mice results in significantly reduced inflammatory cell infiltrate around bronchial airways and perivascular regions, and reduced systemic RANTES levels.

claim: RSV is a leading cause of serious lower respiratory tract illness in infants.
source: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), an enveloped RNA virus of the Pneumoviridae family, is a leading cause of serious lower respiratory tract illness in infants and a potent respiratory pathogen in elderly and immunosuppressed adults (Nair et al., 2010; Hall et al., 2009), leading to more deaths each year worldwide than influenza.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nair et al., 2010 and Hall et al., 2009.

claim: RSV is a potent respiratory pathogen in elderly and immunosuppressed adults.
source: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), an enveloped RNA virus of the Pneumoviridae family, is a leading cause of serious lower respiratory tract illness in infants and a potent respiratory pathogen in elderly and immunosuppressed adults (Nair et al., 2010; Hall et al., 2009), leading to more deaths each year worldwide than influenza.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nair et al., 2010 and Hall et al., 2009.

claim: There are no effective anti-RSV therapeutics generally available.
source: Despite this, there are no effective anti-RSV therapeutics generally available, with palivizumab (Synagis) and ribavirin the only approved agents as a prophylactic and therapeutic, respectively, for high-risk patients (Hurwitz, 2011; Hebert and Guglielmo, 1990; Resch, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a fact with citations supporting the limited approved agents.

claim: Palivizumab (Synagis) is the only approved prophylactic agent for high-risk RSV patients.
source: Despite this, there are no effective anti-RSV therapeutics generally available, with palivizumab (Synagis) and ribavirin the only approved agents as a prophylactic and therapeutic, respectively, for high-risk patients (Hurwitz, 2011; Hebert and Guglielmo, 1990; Resch, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hurwitz, 2011; Hebert and Guglielmo, 1990; Resch, 2017.

claim: Ribavirin is the only approved therapeutic agent for high-risk RSV patients.
source: Despite this, there are no effective anti-RSV therapeutics generally available, with palivizumab (Synagis) and ribavirin the only approved agents as a prophylactic and therapeutic, respectively, for high-risk patients (Hurwitz, 2011; Hebert and Guglielmo, 1990; Resch, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hurwitz, 2011; Hebert and Guglielmo, 1990; Resch, 2017.

claim: RSV replicates in the cytoplasm.
source: Like all pneumoviruses, RSV replicates in the cytoplasm (Collins et al., 2013), but specific interaction with host cell organelles, and the mitochondria in particular, has remained largely unexplored.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Collins et al., 2013.

claim: RSV infection impacts the abundance of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins.
source: Unbiased discovery studies capitalising on quantitative proteomic protocols to identify changes in protein levels upon RSV infection have revealed a significant impact on the abundance of a number of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins (Munday et al., 2015; van Diepen et al., 2010; Kipper et al., 2015), including respiratory complex I proteins, outer mitochondrial membrane complex subunits, voltage-dependent anion channel protein, and the prohibitin subunits that play essential roles in the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics, morphology and biogenesis (Kipper et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Munday et al., 2015; van Diepen et al., 2010; Kipper et al., 2015.

claim: RSV infection affects respiratory complex I proteins.
source: Unbiased discovery studies capitalising on quantitative proteomic protocols to identify changes in protein levels upon RSV infection have revealed a significant impact on the abundance of a number of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins (Munday et al., 2015; van Diepen et al., 2010; Kipper et al., 2015), including respiratory complex I proteins, outer mitochondrial membrane complex subunits, voltage-dependent anion channel protein, and the prohibitin subunits that play essential roles in the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics, morphology and biogenesis (Kipper et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous proteomic studies.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation is responsible for up to 90% of cellular ATP production.
source: Oxidative phosphorylation driven by ATP synthase/complex V and the electron transport chain (complexes I-IV) is responsible for up to 90% of cellular ATP production (Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016.

claim: ROS arising from incomplete electron transfer across complexes I and III are generally cleared by intracellular antioxidant enzymes under normal conditions.
source: ROS arising from incomplete electron transfer across complexes I and III are generally cleared by intracellular antioxidant enzymes under normal conditions (Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016), but oxidative stress can occur when ROS production exceeds antioxidant capacity (Lin and Beal, 2006; Schieber and Chandel, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016.

claim: Oxidative stress can occur when ROS production exceeds antioxidant capacity.
source: ROS arising from incomplete electron transfer across complexes I and III are generally cleared by intracellular antioxidant enzymes under normal conditions (Schertl and Braun, 2014; Letts et al., 2016), but oxidative stress can occur when ROS production exceeds antioxidant capacity (Lin and Beal, 2006; Schieber and Chandel, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lin and Beal, 2006; Schieber and Chandel, 2014.

claim: Mitochondria are trafficked intracellularly through the action of molecular motors operating on microtubules and actin filaments.
source: Changes in cytoskeletal organization and/or motor activities can impact mitochondrial distribution and function because mitochondria are trafficked intracellularly through the action of molecular motors operating on microtubules and actin filaments (Welte, 2004; Hancock, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Welte, 2004; Hancock, 2014.

claim: RSV infection results in a higher percentage of cells showing fragmented mitochondrial morphology compared to uninfected cells.
source: Mock- and RSV-infected cells exhibited fragmented, tubular and fibrillar morphologies as revealed by MitoTrackerRed staining (Figure 1A), with a higher percentage of infected cells showing fragmented morphology, and a lower percentage with tubular and fibrillar morphologies, compared to uninfected cells (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: Figure 1B shows quantification demonstrating a significant >30% increase of cells showing fragmented mitochondrial morphology following infection.

claim: RSV infection results in a lower percentage of cells with tubular and fibrillar mitochondrial morphologies compared to uninfected cells.
source: Mock- and RSV-infected cells exhibited fragmented, tubular and fibrillar morphologies as revealed by MitoTrackerRed staining (Figure 1A), with a higher percentage of infected cells showing fragmented morphology, and a lower percentage with tubular and fibrillar morphologies, compared to uninfected cells (Hu et al., 2013).
evidence: Figure 1B shows quantification of mitochondrial morphologies with decreased tubular and fibrillar percentages in RSV-infected cells.

claim: RSV infection causes a significant >30% increase of cells showing fragmented mitochondrial morphology at 8 h p.i.
source: Quantitative analysis confirmed the observations, with a significant (p<0.001)>30% increase of cells showing fragmented mitochondrial morphology following infection, compared to mock infected cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows quantitative data with statistical significance indicated.

claim: The Golgi apparatus remains asymmetrically close to the nuclei in both mock- and RSV-infected cells.
source: To confirm that the effects on host mitochondria are specific, we also tested for changes in the Golgi apparatus by staining using the CellLight Golgi-GFP *BacMam 2.0* (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The Golgi cisterna remained asymmetrically close to the nuclei in mock- and RSV-infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in stark contrast to the striking changes in mitochondria at 8 and 24 h p.i.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows Golgi staining that does not change with RSV infection, serving as a control.

claim: RSV infection specifically reorganizes host cell mitochondria with perinuclear clustering followed by MTOC-oriented asymmetry.
source: Together, these findings indicate that RSV infection specifically reorganizes the host cell mitochondria, with perinuclear clustering followed by MTOC-oriented asymmetry.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the imaging data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: RSV induces perinuclear mitochondrial clustering in human airway basal cells (BCi-NS1).
source: BCi-NS1 cells were infected with RSV for 18 or 36 h p.i. (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A). In contrast to the even distribution of mitochondria throughout the mock-infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; first two rows), substantial perinuclear mitochondrial clustering was observed in RSV-infected cells at 18 and 36 hr (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; 3rd and 4th rows), completely consistent with our observations in A549 cells (Figure 1).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows imaging and quantitative analysis in BCi-NS1 cells demonstrating perinuclear clustering.

claim: R90% is significantly reduced by over 30% in RSV-infected BCi-NS1 cells at 18 or 36 h p.i. compared to mock-infected cells.
source: Quantitative analysis of the R90% parameter (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) confirmed these observations, whereby R90% was significantly (p<0.01) reduced (over 30%) in RSV-infected cells at 18 or 36 h p.i., compared to mock-infected cells.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2B shows quantitative data with statistical significance.

claim: RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering is strongly dependent on the integrity of the microtubule network.
source: Significantly, RSV-infected cells continued to show perinuclear clustering of mitochondria following treatment with cytochalasin D (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C) but not with nocodazole (Figure 3A, Figure 3 - Figure 1—video 3), confirming that RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering is strongly dependent on the integrity of the microtubule network but not the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: Figure 3A and 3B show that nocodazole treatment prevents mitochondrial clustering while cytochalasin D does not.

claim: RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering is not dependent on the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Significantly, RSV-infected cells continued to show perinuclear clustering of mitochondria following treatment with cytochalasin D (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C) but not with nocodazole (Figure 3A, Figure 3 - Figure 1—video 3), confirming that RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering is strongly dependent on the integrity of the microtubule network but not the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 3 shows that cytochalasin D treatment does not prevent mitochondrial clustering.

claim: RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering relies on dynein-dependent retrograde transport along intact microtubules.
source: Strikingly, RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering was completely abolished by treatment with EHNA but not monastrol. Quantitative analysis for the R90% parameter confirmed this finding (Figure 3B), indicating that RSV-induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering relies on dynein-dependent retrograde transport along intact microtubules.
evidence: Figure 3A and 3B show that EHNA (dynein inhibitor) prevents clustering while monastrol (kinesin inhibitor) does not.

claim: RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering is suppressed by depletion of DYNLT1.
source: Consistent with the effects for EHNA above, RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering was suppressed by depletion of either DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1, resulting in an even distribution of reticular mitochondria (Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3D and 3E show that siRNA knockdown of DYNLT1 prevents mitochondrial clustering.

claim: RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering is suppressed by depletion of DYNC1H1.
source: Consistent with the effects for EHNA above, RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering was suppressed by depletion of either DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1, resulting in an even distribution of reticular mitochondria (Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3D and 3E show that siRNA knockdown of DYNC1H1 prevents mitochondrial clustering.

claim: RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering is not affected by depletion of KLC1.
source: In contrast, RSV-induced perinuclear mitochondrial clustering was not affected by depletion of KLC1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Figure 3D and 3E show that siRNA knockdown of KLC1 does not prevent mitochondrial clustering.

claim: Nocodazole treatment prevents MTOC-oriented mitochondrial asymmetry at 18 hr RSV infection.
source: We extended our analysis to the RSV-induced mitochondrial asymmetry that follows mitochondrial perinuclear clustering, finding that nocodazole and EHNA treatments prevent the MTOC-oriented mitochondrial asymmetry characteristic of longer (18 hr) RSV infection (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A, 4B, and 4C show that nocodazole treatment prevents MTOC-oriented mitochondrial distribution.

claim: EHNA treatment prevents MTOC-oriented mitochondrial asymmetry at 18 hr RSV infection.
source: We extended our analysis to the RSV-induced mitochondrial asymmetry that follows mitochondrial perinuclear clustering, finding that nocodazole and EHNA treatments prevent the MTOC-oriented mitochondrial asymmetry characteristic of longer (18 hr) RSV infection (Figure 4A).
evidence: Figure 4A, 4B, and 4C show that EHNA treatment prevents MTOC-oriented mitochondrial distribution.

claim: RSV-induced mitochondrial redistribution is dynein/microtubule-dependent.
source: Quantitative analysis for the angular mitochondrial distribution (Figure 4B–4C) supported this conclusion, results overall demonstrating a dynein/microtubule-dependent mechanism underlying RSV-induced mitochondrial redistribution during the course of infection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figures 3 and 4 showing effects of microtubule and dynein inhibition.

claim: OCR progressively decreases during RSV infection from 6-24 hr.
source: We used the Seahorse XF96 Extracellular Flux Analyser to measure oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) of living cells over the time course (6–24 hr) of RSV infection (Figure 5A), as indicators of mitochondrial respiration and glycolysis, respectively (Wu et al., 2007). OCR progressively decreased during the RSV infection (Figure 5A, main panel), and was accompanied by increases in ECAR (Figure 5A, inset) indicating an inhibition of mitochondrial respiration and a parallel increase in glycolytic metabolism for energy production.
evidence: Figure 5A shows Seahorse bioenergetics data demonstrating progressive decrease in OCR over time.

claim: ECAR increases during RSV infection from 6-24 hr.
source: OCR progressively decreased during the RSV infection (Figure 5A, main panel), and was accompanied by increases in ECAR (Figure 5A, inset) indicating an inhibition of mitochondrial respiration and a parallel increase in glycolytic metabolism for energy production.
evidence: Figure 5A inset shows correlation of OCR and ECAR with ECAR increasing as OCR decreases.

claim: RSV infection inhibits mitochondrial respiration and increases glycolytic metabolism for energy production.
source: OCR progressively decreased during the RSV infection (Figure 5A, main panel), and was accompanied by increases in ECAR (Figure 5A, inset) indicating an inhibition of mitochondrial respiration and a parallel increase in glycolytic metabolism for energy production.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the OCR and ECAR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Increasing multiplicity of infection (MOI) results in more severe effects on mitochondrial respiration.
source: These effects paralleled the robustness of infection, with increasing multiplicity of infection (MOI) resulting in more severe effects (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and 1C show dose-dependent effects of RSV MOI on respiratory parameters.

claim: RSV infection causes significant decreases in maximal OCR from 8 h p.i.
source: Whilst no significant changes were observed within 6 h p.i., we observed significant decreases in maximal OCR (from 8 h p.i.), basal and ATP-linked OCR (from 18 h p.i.); non-mitochondrial OCR was significantly increased from 8 h p.i. (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows quantitative respiratory parameters with statistical significance indicated.

claim: RSV infection causes significant decreases in basal OCR from 18 h p.i.
source: Whilst no significant changes were observed within 6 h p.i., we observed significant decreases in maximal OCR (from 8 h p.i.), basal and ATP-linked OCR (from 18 h p.i.); non-mitochondrial OCR was significantly increased from 8 h p.i. (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows quantitative respiratory parameters with statistical significance indicated.

claim: RSV infection causes significant decreases in ATP-linked OCR from 18 h p.i.
source: Whilst no significant changes were observed within 6 h p.i., we observed significant decreases in maximal OCR (from 8 h p.i.), basal and ATP-linked OCR (from 18 h p.i.); non-mitochondrial OCR was significantly increased from 8 h p.i. (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows quantitative respiratory parameters with statistical significance indicated.

claim: RSV infection causes significant increases in non-mitochondrial OCR from 8 h p.i.
source: Whilst no significant changes were observed within 6 h p.i., we observed significant decreases in maximal OCR (from 8 h p.i.), basal and ATP-linked OCR (from 18 h p.i.); non-mitochondrial OCR was significantly increased from 8 h p.i. (Figure 5B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows quantitative respiratory parameters with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Nocodazole treatment restores all respiratory activities in RSV-infected cells at 18 h p.i.
source: Strikingly, all respiratory activities (basal, ATP-linked, maximal and non-mitochondrial) in the RSV-infected cells treated with nocodazole or EHNA remained unchanged (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows that nocodazole treatment prevents RSV-induced changes in respiratory parameters.

claim: EHNA treatment restores all respiratory activities in RSV-infected cells at 18 h p.i.
source: Strikingly, all respiratory activities (basal, ATP-linked, maximal and non-mitochondrial) in the RSV-infected cells treated with nocodazole or EHNA remained unchanged (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows that EHNA treatment prevents RSV-induced changes in respiratory parameters.

claim: RSV-induced changes in host cell respiration activities are dependent on dynein/microtubules.
source: Together, these results show that the RSV-induced changes in host cell respiration activities are dependent on dynein/microtubules.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 5C showing that inhibiting microtubules or dynein prevents respiratory changes.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration is required to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential Δψm.
source: Mitochondrial respiration is required to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential Δψm (Gottlieb et al., 2003; Dey and Moraes, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gottlieb et al., 2003; Dey and Moraes, 2000.

claim: RSV infection induces a loss of host cell mitochondrial membrane potential Δψm by ~18 h p.i.
source: Thus, by ~18 h p.i., RSV infection induces a loss of host cell mitochondrial membrane potential, Δψm.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the TMRE and TPE-Ph-In imaging data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lower TMRE fluorescence is observed in RSV-infected cells at 18 and 24 h p.i.
source: Lower TMRE fluorescence was observed in RSV-infected cells at 18 and 24 h p.i., an impact strikingly apparent when infected cells were imaged alongside non-infected cells in the same field (Figure 6A, 5th and 6th rows of panels).
evidence: Figure 6A shows live cell imaging with TMRE demonstrating reduced fluorescence in infected cells.

claim: Δψm is significantly reduced at 18 h p.i. in RSV-infected cells.
source: Quantification of the integrated density of TMRE fluorescence confirmed the results, revealing significantly reduced (p<0.001) Δψm at 18 h p.i. (Figure 6B).
evidence: Figure 6B shows quantification of TMRE fluorescence with statistical significance indicated.

claim: TPE-Ph-In fluorescence shows progressive loss from 16 to 18 h p.i. in RSV-infected cells.
source: To monitor these RSV-induced changes in Δψm over the period of 16–18 h p.i. in real time, we used the photobleach-resistant Δψm-sensitive dye tetraphenylethylene-phenyl-indolium salt (TPE-Ph-In) (Zhao et al., 2015), documenting that TPE-Ph-In fluorescence was maintained throughout the 2 hr imaging period in mock-infected cells, but showed a progressive loss of TPE-Ph-In fluorescence at 16 to 18 h p.i. in RSV-infected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 1 shows time-lapse imaging with TPE-Ph-In demonstrating progressive loss of signal in infected cells.

claim: RSV infection increases mitochondrial ROS generation significantly by 18 h p.i.
source: Quantitative analysis of the ratiometric images highlighted the extent of ROS production (Figure 7B), with the results indicating that RSV infection increases mitochondrial ROS generation significantly (p<0.001) by 18 h p.i.
evidence: Figure 7B shows quantification of FRR2 ratiometric imaging with statistical significance indicated.

claim: MitoQ suppresses rotenone-induced mitochondrial ROS production.
source: We treated mock-infected cells with rotenone as a positive control, with strong FRR2 emission in regions colocalizing with Mitotracker Deep Red (Figure 7A, 3rd row of panels), indicative of high levels of mitochondrial ROS. To confirm the mitochondrial contribution to this staining, we used the mitochondrial ROS scavenger mitoquinone mesylate (MitoQ) (Smith and Murphy, 2010; Maharjan et al., 2014), which strongly suppresses the actions of rotenone (Figure 7A, 4th row of panels).
evidence: Figure 7A shows that MitoQ treatment reduces FRR2 signal in rotenone-treated cells.

claim: MitoQ reduces RSV-induced mitochondrial ROS production.
source: FRR2 fluorescence increased in RSV-infected cells, but was also reduced by MitoQ (Figure 7A; bottom 4 rows of panels).
evidence: Figure 7A and 7B show that MitoQ treatment reduces FRR2 signal in RSV-infected cells.

claim: RSV infection increases population 1 (high ROS) cells by about 2-fold at 8 hr and 8-fold at 18 hr compared to mock infection.
source: Compared to mock infection, RSV infection at 8 and 18 hr increased population 1 by about 2- and 8-fold, respectively, with these increases reversed by MitoQ (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7C shows FACS analysis quantifying populations with high and low ROS.

claim: MitoQ reverses RSV-induced increases in high ROS cell populations.
source: Compared to mock infection, RSV infection at 8 and 18 hr increased population 1 by about 2- and 8-fold, respectively, with these increases reversed by MitoQ (Figure 7C).
evidence: Figure 7C shows FACS analysis demonstrating MitoQ reduces the high ROS population in infected cells.

claim: Higher levels of ROS are associated with perinuclear mitochondria at 8 h p.i.
source: Analysis of RSV-infected cells revealed higher levels of ROS associated with perinuclear mitochondria at 8 h p.i.; this staining at 12 h p.i. was still perinuclear, but with intense nuclear staining as well as some diffuse cytoplasmic staining (Figure 7D).
evidence: Figure 7D shows DCF staining colocalizing with perinuclear mitochondria at 8 h p.i.

claim: At 12 h p.i., ROS staining is perinuclear with intense nuclear staining and some diffuse cytoplasmic staining.
source: Analysis of RSV-infected cells revealed higher levels of ROS associated with perinuclear mitochondria at 8 h p.i.; this staining at 12 h p.i. was still perinuclear, but with intense nuclear staining as well as some diffuse cytoplasmic staining (Figure 7D).
evidence: Figure 7D shows DCF staining pattern at 12 h p.i.

claim: MitoQ markedly reduces DCF staining in RSV-infected cells.
source: We then treated RSV-infected cells with MitoQ 2 hr before imaging and observed a marked reduction in DCF staining, suggesting that the ROS generated in the absence of MitoQ in infected cells was largely mitochondrial (Figure 7D).
evidence: Figure 7D shows reduced DCF staining with MitoQ treatment in infected cells.

claim: ROS generated in RSV-infected cells is largely mitochondrial.
source: We then treated RSV-infected cells with MitoQ 2 hr before imaging and observed a marked reduction in DCF staining, suggesting that the ROS generated in the absence of MitoQ in infected cells was largely mitochondrial (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that MitoQ, a mitochondria-specific ROS scavenger, reduces DCF staining.

claim: Nocodazole treatment prevents nuclear accumulation of ROS in RSV-infected cells.
source: Strikingly, when we included nocodazole treatment to prevent microtubule-dependent mitochondrial clustering upon RSV infection, DCF staining remained largely mitochondrial and cytoplasmic and was largely excluded from the nucleus (Figure 7D, bottom row).
evidence: Figure 7D shows that nocodazole treatment changes the pattern of DCF staining, keeping it cytoplasmic rather than nuclear.

claim: Mitochondrial perinuclear redistribution is a prerequisite for altering the oxidative status of the host cell nucleus during RSV infection.
source: An implication of these findings is that mitochondrial perinuclear redistribution is a prerequisite for altering the oxidative status of the host cell nucleus during RSV infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that preventing mitochondrial redistribution with nocodazole prevents nuclear ROS accumulation.

claim: Addition of MitoQ at 8 or 18 h p.i. reduces viral genome replication by up to 60% at 24 h p.i.
source: Excitingly, addition of MitoQ at 8 or even 18 h p.i. had a significant (p<0.001) inhibitory effect, reducing viral genome replication by up to 60% and infectious virus production by up to 3.5 logs measured at 24 h p.i. (Figure 7E).
evidence: Figure 7E shows qPCR data demonstrating reduced viral RNA copy numbers with MitoQ treatment.

claim: Addition of MitoQ at 8 or 18 h p.i. reduces infectious virus production by up to 3.5 logs at 24 h p.i.
source: Excitingly, addition of MitoQ at 8 or even 18 h p.i. had a significant (p<0.001) inhibitory effect, reducing viral genome replication by up to 60% and infectious virus production by up to 3.5 logs measured at 24 h p.i. (Figure 7E).
evidence: Figure 7E shows plaque assay data demonstrating reduced infectious virus with MitoQ treatment.

claim: Mitochondrial ROS production contributes essentially to RSV virus production.
source: These results confirm that mitochondrial ROS production contributes essentially to RSV virus production, and that MitoQ, as a specific inhibitor of mitochondrial ROS, is a potent inhibitor of RSV infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MitoQ inhibition data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: MitoQ is a potent inhibitor of RSV infection.
source: These results confirm that mitochondrial ROS production contributes essentially to RSV virus production, and that MitoQ, as a specific inhibitor of mitochondrial ROS, is a potent inhibitor of RSV infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MitoQ inhibition data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: MitoQ does not alter the density or size of syncytia formed at 48 h p.i.
source: MitoQ was found not to alter the density or size of syncytia formed at 48 h p.i. (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that mitochondrial ROS generation facilitates infectious virus production by promoting viral replication rather than enhancing virus spread to neighboring uninfected cells through cell fusion.
evidence: Figure 7—figure supplement 1B shows quantification of syncytia with no significant difference with MitoQ treatment.

claim: Mitochondrial ROS generation facilitates infectious virus production by promoting viral replication rather than enhancing virus spread through cell fusion.
source: MitoQ was found not to alter the density or size of syncytia formed at 48 h p.i. (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that mitochondrial ROS generation facilitates infectious virus production by promoting viral replication rather than enhancing virus spread to neighboring uninfected cells through cell fusion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MitoQ reduces virus production but does not affect syncytia formation.

claim: Microtubule and dynein are necessary for the formation of RSV infectious virus filaments.
source: Previous studies have indicated that microtubule and dynein are necessary for the formation of RSV infectious virus filaments (Vanover et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Vanover et al., 2017.

claim: Treatment with nocodazole significantly reduces infectious virus production by up to 2.5 log.
source: Treatment with the microtubule/dynein motor targeting agents nocodazole or EHNA significantly (p<0.05) reduced (up to 2.5 log) infectious virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the actin-targeted agent cytochalasin D or the kinesin-inhibitor monastrol that had no significant effect.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows plaque assay data with nocodazole treatment.

claim: Treatment with EHNA significantly reduces infectious virus production by up to 2.5 log.
source: Treatment with the microtubule/dynein motor targeting agents nocodazole or EHNA significantly (p<0.05) reduced (up to 2.5 log) infectious virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the actin-targeted agent cytochalasin D or the kinesin-inhibitor monastrol that had no significant effect.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows plaque assay data with EHNA treatment.

claim: Cytochalasin D has no significant effect on infectious virus production.
source: Treatment with the microtubule/dynein motor targeting agents nocodazole or EHNA significantly (p<0.05) reduced (up to 2.5 log) infectious virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the actin-targeted agent cytochalasin D or the kinesin-inhibitor monastrol that had no significant effect.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows plaque assay data with cytochalasin D treatment showing no significant effect.

claim: Monastrol has no significant effect on infectious virus production.
source: Treatment with the microtubule/dynein motor targeting agents nocodazole or EHNA significantly (p<0.05) reduced (up to 2.5 log) infectious virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), in contrast to the actin-targeted agent cytochalasin D or the kinesin-inhibitor monastrol that had no significant effect.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows plaque assay data with monastrol treatment showing no significant effect.

claim: siRNA-knockdown of DYNLT1 results in significant decreases in infectious virus production (2-3 logs).
source: Similarly, siRNA-knockdown of proteins of the dynein complex (DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), but not the kinesin complex (KLC1), resulted in significant (p<0.001) decreases in infectious virus production (2–3 logs) compared to the scrambled siRNA control (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows plaque assay data with DYNLT1 siRNA knockdown.

claim: siRNA-knockdown of DYNC1H1 results in significant decreases in infectious virus production (2-3 logs).
source: Similarly, siRNA-knockdown of proteins of the dynein complex (DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), but not the kinesin complex (KLC1), resulted in significant (p<0.001) decreases in infectious virus production (2–3 logs) compared to the scrambled siRNA control (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows plaque assay data with DYNC1H1 siRNA knockdown.

claim: siRNA-knockdown of KLC1 does not result in significant decreases in infectious virus production.
source: Similarly, siRNA-knockdown of proteins of the dynein complex (DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), but not the kinesin complex (KLC1), resulted in significant (p<0.001) decreases in infectious virus production (2–3 logs) compared to the scrambled siRNA control (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1B shows plaque assay data with KLC1 siRNA knockdown showing no significant effect.

claim: Mitochondrial reorganization, rather than the microtubule network per se, is key to RSV infection.
source: None of the treatments above impacting mitochondrial distribution induced by RSV infection, apart from nocodazole, impact microtubules directly (see Figure 3AD), implying that mitochondrial redistribution, rather than the microtubule network per se, is key to RSV infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EHNA and dynein siRNAs, which don't affect microtubule structure, still inhibit virus production.

claim: CLUH plays a key role in mitochondrial distribution independent of the microtubule network.
source: To examine this idea further, we performed knockdown experiments for the mRNA-binding protein CLUH (clustered mitochondria homolog) (Figure 8A), which plays a key role in mitochondrial distribution independent of the microtubule network by facilitating translation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes close to mitochondria (Wakim et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wakim et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2014.

claim: CLUH-targeting siRNA induces mitochondrial perinuclear clustering in mock infected cells.
source: As observed previously (Wakim et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2014), CLUH-targeting siRNA but not control scrambled siRNA induced mitochondrial perinuclear clustering in mock infected cells (Figure 8B; first two rows), with RSV-infection resulting in only a further slight increase in clustering (Figure 8B; 4th row).
evidence: Figure 8B and 8C show imaging and quantification demonstrating CLUH knockdown induces clustering.

claim: CLUH knockdown-induced mitochondrial redistribution results in elevated mitochondrial ROS production.
source: Strikingly, the CLUH knockdown-induced mitochondrial redistribution resulted in elevated mitochondrial ROS production, as indicated by strong FRR2 emission in regions colocalizing with Mitotracker Deep Red as revealed by ratiometric live cell imaging in mock-infected cells (Figure 8D; first two rows); RSV infection further enhanced the effect (Figure 8D; last two rows).
evidence: Figure 8D and 8E show FRR2 ratiometric imaging demonstrating increased ROS with CLUH knockdown.

claim: Depletion of CLUH significantly increases mitochondrial ROS levels in mock- and RSV-infected cells.
source: Quantitative analysis of the ratiometric images confirmed the results, indicating that depletion of CLUH significantly (p<0.01) increased mitochondrial ROS levels in mock- and RSV-infected cells (Figure 8E).
evidence: Figure 8E shows quantification of FRR2 ratios with statistical significance indicated.

claim: siRNA-mediated CLUH knockdown results in significantly increased virus production.
source: Finally, the physiological relevance of these results with respect to the RSV infectious cycle could be confirmed by showing that siRNA-mediated CLUH knockdown resulted in significantly (p<0.01) increased virus production (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1C shows plaque assay data demonstrating increased virus production with CLUH knockdown.

claim: Mitochondrial reorganization is key to RSV infection through its link to mitochondrial ROS production.
source: The results overall confirm that mitochondrial reorganization, rather than the microtubule network per se, is key to RSV infection, through its link to mitochondrial ROS production.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the CLUH knockdown experiments showing that inducing mitochondrial clustering increases both ROS and virus production.

claim: None of the drug treatments significantly increase LDH release compared to controls.
source: None of our drug (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) or siRNA (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B) treatments significantly increased LDH release compared to that of controls in either the absence or presence of infection, consistent with the idea that all of the treatments affecting RSV virus production did so through specific effects on mitochondrial distribution/mitochondrial ROS production, rather than as a result of toxicity.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 2A shows LDH release assay data demonstrating no significant cytotoxicity.

claim: None of the siRNA treatments significantly increase LDH release compared to controls.
source: None of our drug (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) or siRNA (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B) treatments significantly increased LDH release compared to that of controls in either the absence or presence of infection, consistent with the idea that all of the treatments affecting RSV virus production did so through specific effects on mitochondrial distribution/mitochondrial ROS production, rather than as a result of toxicity.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 2B shows LDH release assay data demonstrating no significant cytotoxicity.

claim: Treatments affecting RSV virus production do so through specific effects on mitochondrial distribution/mitochondrial ROS production, rather than as a result of toxicity.
source: None of our drug (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A) or siRNA (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B) treatments significantly increased LDH release compared to that of controls in either the absence or presence of infection, consistent with the idea that all of the treatments affecting RSV virus production did so through specific effects on mitochondrial distribution/mitochondrial ROS production, rather than as a result of toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cytotoxicity shown in the LDH assays.

claim: RSV infection effectively co-opts mitochondria in a microtubule- and dynein-dependent fashion to perinuclear/asymmetric mitochondrial distribution that favours reduced mitochondrial respiration and enhanced mitochondrial ROS production.
source: Together, the results indicate that mitochondrial ROS generation facilitates RSV infection, with RSV infection effectively co-opting mitochondria in a microtubule- and dynein-dependent fashion to perinuclear/asymmetric mitochondrial distribution that favours reduced mitochondrial respiration and enhanced mitochondrial ROS production.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating all the findings from the manuscript.

claim: Blocking RSV induced reorganization of host cell mitochondria and increased mitochondrial ROS production inhibits RSV infection effectively.
source: Blocking RSV induced reorganization of host cell mitochondria and increased mitochondrial ROS production thus inhibits RSV infection effectively.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the inhibition experiments with nocodazole, EHNA, and MitoQ.

claim: MitoQ treatment of RSV-infected pBECs results in significantly reduced viral genomes (>70%) at 18 and 36 h p.i.
source: Whereas RSV infection of the vehicle-treated cells resulted in high levels of viral genomes (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A) and infectious virus titres (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B) at 18 and 36 h p.i., cells treated with MitoQ showed significantly (p<0.001) reduced numbers of viral genomes (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A;>70%) and infectious virus titres (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B;>4 logs) at both timepoints p.i.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 3A shows qPCR data from pBECs with MitoQ treatment.

claim: MitoQ treatment of RSV-infected pBECs results in significantly reduced infectious virus titres (>4 logs) at 18 and 36 h p.i.
source: Whereas RSV infection of the vehicle-treated cells resulted in high levels of viral genomes (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A) and infectious virus titres (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B) at 18 and 36 h p.i., cells treated with MitoQ showed significantly (p<0.001) reduced numbers of viral genomes (Figure 8—figure supplement 3A;>70%) and infectious virus titres (Figure 8—figure supplement 3B;>4 logs) at both timepoints p.i.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 3B shows plaque assay data from pBECs with MitoQ treatment.

claim: Elevated mitochondrial ROS is critical for RSV infection in a clinically relevant human infectious model.
source: These results were consistent with the idea that elevated mitochondrial ROS is critical for RSV infection in a clinically relevant human infectious model.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pBEC data showing MitoQ inhibits infection in primary human cells.

claim: In the BALB/c mouse model, viral replication and infectious virus titres peak at day 5 p.i. and decline rapidly at day 7 p.i.
source: As previously (van Schaik et al., 1998; Taylor et al., 1984), viral replication and infectious virus titres peaked at day 5 p.i., declining rapidly at day 7 p.i. (Figure 9AB, black bars).
evidence: Figure 9A and 9B show viral genome and infectious virus data over time in mice, with citations to previous studies.

claim: MitoQ treatment in mice results in significantly reduced (>4 fold) viral replication for days 4-7 p.i.
source: Mice treated with MitoQ (Figure 9AB, grey bars) showed significantly (p<0.001) reduced (>4 fold) viral replication and infectious virus production compared to the vehicle control for days 4–7 p.i.
evidence: Figure 9A shows qPCR data from mouse lungs with MitoQ treatment.

claim: MitoQ treatment in mice results in significantly reduced infectious virus production for days 4-7 p.i.
source: Mice treated with MitoQ (Figure 9AB, grey bars) showed significantly (p<0.001) reduced (>4 fold) viral replication and infectious virus production compared to the vehicle control for days 4–7 p.i.
evidence: Figure 9B shows plaque assay data from mouse lungs with MitoQ treatment.

claim: MitoQ treatment results in significantly less dense inflammatory cell infiltrate around bronchial airways in mouse lungs.
source: Importantly, MitoQ treatment resulted in significantly (p<0.001) less dense inflammatory cell infiltrate (characterised by mononuclear cells and eosinophils) around the bronchial airways (Figure 9CD) and perivascular regions (Figure 9EF) of the lungs, as revealed by histological sectioning and objective blind assessment (Ford et al., 2001; Mehra et al., 2012).
evidence: Figure 9C and 9D show histology images and quantification of bronchial inflammation with MitoQ treatment.

claim: MitoQ treatment results in significantly less dense inflammatory cell infiltrate around perivascular regions in mouse lungs.
source: Importantly, MitoQ treatment resulted in significantly (p<0.001) less dense inflammatory cell infiltrate (characterised by mononuclear cells and eosinophils) around the bronchial airways (Figure 9CD) and perivascular regions (Figure 9EF) of the lungs, as revealed by histological sectioning and objective blind assessment (Ford et al., 2001; Mehra et al., 2012).
evidence: Figure 9E and 9F show histology images and quantification of perivascular inflammation with MitoQ treatment.

claim: MitoQ treatment results in significantly reduced levels of systemic RANTES chemokine.
source: Consistent with the alleviated host response to infection in the case of MitoQ treatment, we observed significantly (p<0.01) reduced levels of systemic RANTES, a chemokine highly chemoattractant for the inflammatory infiltrate, upon MitoQ administration throughout (Figure 9G).
evidence: Figure 9G shows ELISA data for RANTES levels in mouse serum with MitoQ treatment.

claim: MitoQ treatment suppresses RSV infection and decreases virus-induced inflammation in mice.
source: Taken together, MitoQ treatment suppresses RSV infection and decreases virus-induced inflammation in mice, with clear therapeutic implications.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the mouse data in Figure 9.

claim: RSV drives a staged redistribution of mitochondria in microtubule- and dynein-dependent fashion.
source: This study shows for the first time that RSV infection co-opts host cell mitochondria to favour infection; over an 8–24 hr period of infection, RSV progressively impacts the host cell, with mitochondrial redistribution to a perinuclear location near the MTOC, decreased mitochondrial respiration, a loss of Δψm, and increased mitochondrial ROS generation (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating findings from multiple experiments shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: RSV infection is concomitant with compromised mitochondrial respiration in infected cells.
source: This study shows for the first time that RSV infection co-opts host cell mitochondria to favour infection; over an 8–24 hr period of infection, RSV progressively impacts the host cell, with mitochondrial redistribution to a perinuclear location near the MTOC, decreased mitochondrial respiration, a loss of Δψm, and increased mitochondrial ROS generation (Figure 10).
evidence: Figure 5 shows Seahorse bioenergetics data demonstrating compromised respiration.

claim: Inhibiting RSV-induced changes in mitochondrial distribution restores mitochondrial respiration.
source: Inhibiting RSV-induced changes in mitochondrial distribution both restores mitochondrial respiration, and can protect against RSV infection.
evidence: Figure 5C shows that nocodazole and EHNA treatment restore respiratory parameters in infected cells.

claim: Inhibiting RSV-induced changes in mitochondrial distribution can protect against RSV infection.
source: Inhibiting RSV-induced changes in mitochondrial distribution both restores mitochondrial respiration, and can protect against RSV infection.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1 shows that agents inhibiting mitochondrial redistribution reduce virus production.

claim: RSV's effects on mitochondria result in enhanced mitochondrial ROS production.
source: Further, we show that RSV's effects on the mitochondria result in enhanced mitochondrial ROS production; importantly, blocking mitochondrial ROS with a specific inhibitor significantly reduces RSV replication and titers, and alleviates RSV-induced inflammation in a mouse model.
evidence: Figure 7 shows multiple lines of evidence for enhanced mitochondrial ROS in RSV infection.

claim: Blocking mitochondrial ROS significantly reduces RSV replication and titers.
source: Further, we show that RSV's effects on the mitochondria result in enhanced mitochondrial ROS production; importantly, blocking mitochondrial ROS with a specific inhibitor significantly reduces RSV replication and titers, and alleviates RSV-induced inflammation in a mouse model.
evidence: Figure 7E and Figure 9A-B show that MitoQ reduces viral replication and titers in cells and mice.

claim: Blocking mitochondrial ROS alleviates RSV-induced inflammation in a mouse model.
source: Further, we show that RSV's effects on the mitochondria result in enhanced mitochondrial ROS production; importantly, blocking mitochondrial ROS with a specific inhibitor significantly reduces RSV replication and titers, and alleviates RSV-induced inflammation in a mouse model.
evidence: Figure 9C-G show that MitoQ reduces lung inflammation and systemic RANTES in mice.

claim: RSV co-opts host cell mitochondria to enhance mitochondrial ROS to facilitate virus production.
source: The results highlight RSV's ability to co-opt the host cell mitochondria to enhance mitochondrial ROS to facilitate virus production, and establish it for the first time as a viable target for future anti-RSV strategies.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating all findings from the manuscript.

claim: Host cell mitochondria are established for the first time as a viable target for future anti-RSV strategies.
source: The results highlight RSV's ability to co-opt the host cell mitochondria to enhance mitochondrial ROS to facilitate virus production, and establish it for the first time as a viable target for future anti-RSV strategies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the therapeutic efficacy of MitoQ and other mitochondria-targeting interventions.

claim: Oxidative stress plays a fundamental role in the pathogenesis of RSV-associated lung inflammatory disease.
source: Oxidative stress is known to play a fundamental role in the pathogenesis of RSV-associated lung inflammatory disease, correlating strongly with disease severity (Hosakote et al., 2009; Castro et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hosakote et al., 2009; Castro et al., 2006.

claim: Oxidative stress correlates strongly with RSV disease severity.
source: Oxidative stress is known to play a fundamental role in the pathogenesis of RSV-associated lung inflammatory disease, correlating strongly with disease severity (Hosakote et al., 2009; Castro et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hosakote et al., 2009; Castro et al., 2006.

claim: Progressive increases in lipid peroxidation products occur in parallel with lowered reduced glutathione levels in RSV-infected airway epithelial cells.
source: Significantly, progressive increases in lipid peroxidation products in parallel with lowered reduced glutathione levels in RSV-infected airway epithelial cells indicate the increased oxidative stress in cells following RSV infection (Hosakote et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hosakote et al., 2009.

claim: Antioxidants have been reported to limit RSV infection in cell culture.
source: Antioxidants have been reported to limit RSV infection in cell culture as well as in mouse models (Hosakote et al., 2009; Castro et al., 2006; Komaravelli et al., 2015; Zang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hosakote et al., 2009; Castro et al., 2006; Komaravelli et al., 2015; Zang et al., 2011.

claim: Antioxidants have been reported to limit RSV infection in mouse models.
source: Antioxidants have been reported to limit RSV infection in cell culture as well as in mouse models (Hosakote et al., 2009; Castro et al., 2006; Komaravelli et al., 2015; Zang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hosakote et al., 2009; Castro et al., 2006; Komaravelli et al., 2015; Zang et al., 2011.

claim: Modulation of oxidative stress in the context of RSV infection can help diminish lung disease.
source: This study shows for the first time that treatment with an agent specifically scavenging mitochondrial ROS can limit viremia, significantly reduce levels of RANTES chemokine and ameliorate lung and systemic inflammation (Figure 9), implying that modulation of oxidative stress in the context of RSV infection can help diminish lung disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the mouse data showing MitoQ reduces inflammation and disease markers.

claim: Butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) can reduce levels of RANTES chemokine and lung inflammation in RSV-infected mice.
source: This is consistent with the work of Castro et al. (2006), who showed that the antioxidant butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) can reduce levels of chemokine (RANTES) and lung inflammation in RSV-infected mice, as well as the fact that antioxidants have been reported to help alleviate symptoms in paediatric patients with clinical RSV infection (Dowell et al., 1996; Kawasaki et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Castro et al., 2006.

claim: Antioxidants have been reported to help alleviate symptoms in paediatric patients with clinical RSV infection.
source: This is consistent with the work of Castro et al. (2006), who showed that the antioxidant butylated hydroxyanisole (BHA) can reduce levels of chemokine (RANTES) and lung inflammation in RSV-infected mice, as well as the fact that antioxidants have been reported to help alleviate symptoms in paediatric patients with clinical RSV infection (Dowell et al., 1996; Kawasaki et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dowell et al., 1996; Kawasaki et al., 1999.

claim: Mounting evidence highlights the potential of antioxidants to attenuate symptoms and pathology in RSV infection.
source: Thus, mounting evidence highlights the potential of antioxidants to attenuate symptoms and pathology in RSV infection.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the cited literature and the current study's findings.

claim: Agents that inhibit microtubule-/dynein-dependent mitochondrial redistribution limit RSV infection.
source: Specifically, the study shows for the first time that agents that inhibit microtubule-/dynein-dependent mitochondrial redistribution and/or reduce mitochondrial ROS limit RSV infection, with MitoQ in particular able to decrease viremia and airway inflammation in mice.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figures 3, 4, and 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Agents that reduce mitochondrial ROS limit RSV infection.
source: Specifically, the study shows for the first time that agents that inhibit microtubule-/dynein-dependent mitochondrial redistribution and/or reduce mitochondrial ROS limit RSV infection, with MitoQ in particular able to decrease viremia and airway inflammation in mice.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Figures 7 and 9.

claim: MitoQ is able to decrease viremia and airway inflammation in mice.
source: Specifically, the study shows for the first time that agents that inhibit microtubule-/dynein-dependent mitochondrial redistribution and/or reduce mitochondrial ROS limit RSV infection, with MitoQ in particular able to decrease viremia and airway inflammation in mice.
evidence: Figure 9 shows that MitoQ reduces viral load and inflammation in mouse lungs.

claim: MitoQ has been safely delivered in oral form to patients for up to a year in two phase II clinical trials.
source: Significantly, MitoQ has been safely delivered in oral form to patients for up to a year as indicated by two phase II clinical trials (Smith and Murphy, 2010; Maharjan et al., 2014); clearly, the findings introduce the possibility of using MitoQ or a similar antioxidant as an effective anti-RSV agent.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Smith and Murphy, 2010; Maharjan et al., 2014.

claim: The findings introduce the possibility of using MitoQ or a similar antioxidant as an effective anti-RSV agent.
source: Significantly, MitoQ has been safely delivered in oral form to patients for up to a year as indicated by two phase II clinical trials (Smith and Murphy, 2010; Maharjan et al., 2014); clearly, the findings introduce the possibility of using MitoQ or a similar antioxidant as an effective anti-RSV agent.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the safety data from clinical trials and the efficacy data from this study.

claim: Therapeutic modulation of host cell mitochondrial ROS production presents itself as an exciting possibility to counteract RSV infection.
source: Therapeutic modulation of host cell mitochondrial ROS production thus presents itself as an exciting possibility to counteract RSV infection.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on all the findings demonstrating the importance of mitochondrial ROS in RSV infection.

claim: The mechanism by which elevated ROS contributes to RSV infection may in part relate to effects at the level of the nucleus.
source: The mechanism by which elevated ROS contributes to RSV infection may in part relate to effects at the level of the nucleus, with nuclear ROS (eg. see Figure 7D) impacting host nuclear gene transcription (Munday et al., 2015; van Diepen et al., 2010; Kipper et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation of nuclear ROS and citations to studies showing transcriptional changes.

claim: Nuclear ROS impacts host nuclear gene transcription during RSV infection.
source: The mechanism by which elevated ROS contributes to RSV infection may in part relate to effects at the level of the nucleus, with nuclear ROS (eg. see Figure 7D) impacting host nuclear gene transcription (Munday et al., 2015; van Diepen et al., 2010; Kipper et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to proteomic studies and the observation of nuclear ROS in Figure 7D.

claim: RSV infection at 8 h p.i. shows perinuclear mitochondrial clustering.
source: RSV infection induces changes in mitochondrial organization with mitochondrial perinuclear clustering early in infection (8–12 h p.i.), followed by asymmetric distribution of mitochondria close to the MTOC later in infection (18–24 h p.i.)
evidence: Figure 1 and Figure 10 show perinuclear clustering at 8 h p.i.

claim: RSV infection at 12 h p.i. shows perinuclear mitochondrial clustering.
source: RSV infection induces changes in mitochondrial organization with mitochondrial perinuclear clustering early in infection (8–12 h p.i.), followed by asymmetric distribution of mitochondria close to the MTOC later in infection (18–24 h p.i.)
evidence: Figure 1 and Figure 10 show perinuclear clustering at 12 h p.i.

claim: RSV infection at 18 h p.i. shows asymmetric distribution of mitochondria close to the MTOC.
source: RSV infection induces changes in mitochondrial organization with mitochondrial perinuclear clustering early in infection (8–12 h p.i.), followed by asymmetric distribution of mitochondria close to the MTOC later in infection (18–24 h p.i.)
evidence: Figure 2 and Figure 10 show MTOC-oriented asymmetry at 18 h p.i.

claim: RSV infection at 24 h p.i. shows asymmetric distribution of mitochondria close to the MTOC.

claim: Both phases of mitochondrial redistribution (perinuclear clustering and MTOC-oriented asymmetry) are dependent on dynein components.
source: both phases of mitochondrial redistribution (top) are dependent on dynein components (inhibited by siRNAs directed at DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), with perinuclear clustering limited by CLUH (siRNA directed at CLUH increases perinuclear clustering, as well as mitochondrial ROS production and RSV virus production).
evidence: Figures 3 and 4 show that dynein inhibition or knockdown prevents both clustering and asymmetry.

claim: siRNA directed at CLUH increases perinuclear clustering.
source: both phases of mitochondrial redistribution (top) are dependent on dynein components (inhibited by siRNAs directed at DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), with perinuclear clustering limited by CLUH (siRNA directed at CLUH increases perinuclear clustering, as well as mitochondrial ROS production and RSV virus production).
evidence: Figure 8B and 8C show that CLUH knockdown increases clustering.

claim: siRNA directed at CLUH increases mitochondrial ROS production.
source: both phases of mitochondrial redistribution (top) are dependent on dynein components (inhibited by siRNAs directed at DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), with perinuclear clustering limited by CLUH (siRNA directed at CLUH increases perinuclear clustering, as well as mitochondrial ROS production and RSV virus production).
evidence: Figure 8D and 8E show that CLUH knockdown increases mitochondrial ROS.

claim: siRNA directed at CLUH increases RSV virus production.
source: both phases of mitochondrial redistribution (top) are dependent on dynein components (inhibited by siRNAs directed at DYNLT1 or DYNC1H1), with perinuclear clustering limited by CLUH (siRNA directed at CLUH increases perinuclear clustering, as well as mitochondrial ROS production and RSV virus production).
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1C shows that CLUH knockdown increases virus production.

claim: RSV infection inhibits host mitochondrial respiration.
source: Accompanying these changes, RSV infection inhibits host mitochondrial respiration, disrupts maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and enhances mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation.
evidence: Figure 5 shows decreased mitochondrial respiration parameters with RSV infection.

claim: RSV infection disrupts maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm).
source: Accompanying these changes, RSV infection inhibits host mitochondrial respiration, disrupts maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and enhances mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation.
evidence: Figure 6 shows decreased Δψm with RSV infection.

claim: RSV infection enhances mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation.
source: Accompanying these changes, RSV infection inhibits host mitochondrial respiration, disrupts maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψm) and enhances mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation.
evidence: Figure 7 shows increased mitochondrial ROS with RSV infection.

claim: These events (mitochondrial redistribution, decreased respiration, loss of Δψm, increased ROS) favour RSV infection.
source: These events favour RSV infection as indicated by fact that RSV infectious virus production is decreased by disrupting microtubule organization using nocodazole (NCZ), by inhibiting the dynein-motor with EHNA, or using the mitochondrially-targeted antioxidant MitoQ.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that preventing these events reduces virus production.

claim: RSV infectious virus production is decreased by disrupting microtubule organization using nocodazole.
source: These events favour RSV infection as indicated by fact that RSV infectious virus production is decreased by disrupting microtubule organization using nocodazole (NCZ), by inhibiting the dynein-motor with EHNA, or using the mitochondrially-targeted antioxidant MitoQ.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows that nocodazole reduces virus production.

claim: RSV infectious virus production is decreased by inhibiting the dynein-motor with EHNA.
source: These events favour RSV infection as indicated by fact that RSV infectious virus production is decreased by disrupting microtubule organization using nocodazole (NCZ), by inhibiting the dynein-motor with EHNA, or using the mitochondrially-targeted antioxidant MitoQ.
evidence: Figure 8—figure supplement 1A shows that EHNA reduces virus production.

claim: RSV infectious virus production is decreased by using the mitochondrially-targeted antioxidant MitoQ.
source: These events favour RSV infection as indicated by fact that RSV infectious virus production is decreased by disrupting microtubule organization using nocodazole (NCZ), by inhibiting the dynein-motor with EHNA, or using the mitochondrially-targeted antioxidant MitoQ.
